title: Pharmaceutical stocks: how to analyze pharma companies
description: Pharmaceutical stocks: two analyses — developers on pipeline and cash, commercial firms on patents and revenues. The method, examples, sources.
author: AK1A Research Lab
body:
Pharmaceutical stocks are shares in companies that develop, manufacture and sell medicines — from global giants with hundreds of products to small biotechs whose entire value lives in a single molecule not yet approved. That span is the industry's first analytical fact: a commercial company with steady revenues is analyzed with ordinary measures, a development company without revenues on its pipeline, its cash and its time.

What both share is the patent. A medicine's exclusivity is a clock that starts ticking at the application, and the company's value depends on how much earning fits before it strikes. This guide goes through both company types, the chain from molecule to approval and the role of the patent — with worked examples and sources. As always here: education in method, never advice about individual stocks. Ten of the 109 companies in AK1A's analysis universe are healthcare companies — AstraZeneca and Novo Nordisk, but also medtech like Getinge and Elekta — and the course [the Pharma Sector](/kurser/km-039-pharmasektorn) builds out every part.

## Two kinds of pharmaceutical stocks — two methods

The commercial pharmaceutical company has approved products and revenues. Ordinary measures apply again: growth per product and geography, operating margin, P/E against peers — with one addition missing in most industries: every bestseller has an expiry date. The patent turns the revenue stream into a loan on time, not a perpetual machine.

The development company — the biotech — lacks revenues. The income statement is almost meaningless: the loss is by construction (research money is being burned), not a sign of failure. The analysis stands on two legs instead: what the pipeline can become worth, and whether the cash lasts. The second leg is pure arithmetic — cash divided by the burn rate gives the runway, the quarters before the next capital raise; the craft is in [Capital burn — runway](/kurser/rk-01-kapitalforbranning).

## The development chain — from molecule to approval

The chain has fixed steps. Preclinical research is followed by clinical trials in three phases: phase I tests safety in a few healthy volunteers, phase II effect and dose in patients, phase III efficacy in thousands of patients against comparator treatment. Then the application is filed with the authority — in Europe EMA, in the US FDA. The whole chain regularly takes more than a decade and costs in the billions per approved medicine.

The odds are the industry's core number. Of the projects entering clinical phases, on the order of one in ten reaches approval — higher for projects through phase III, lower for those that recently left the laboratory. Every readout of study data is therefore a catalyst with an essentially binary outcome: the primary endpoint is met or not, and share price moves of tens of percent in both directions are everyday events. Few industries have single decisions that move value this much. The event types are systematized in [Regulatory catalysts](/kurser/v18-regulatoriska).

## The patent — the revenue clock

A patent gives at most 20 years of protection from the application. Development time eats into it: a medicine patented in 2020 and approved in 2034 has six years of commercial exclusivity left when sales begin. When protection expires, generics arrive — the same substance at a lower price — and revenues for a product losing exclusivity fall sharply, often by more than half within a few years. The industry's word for it is the patent cliff.

For the analysis the clock means three things. Revenue forecasts must have expiry dates, otherwise they extrapolate a growing eternity that does not exist. The pipeline is the company's timetable — new products must take over where old ones cliff, and gaps are visible in advance. And the multiple is read with the clock — a company with a large cliff imminent often trades lower, not automatically cheap. The anatomy of patents — application dates, protection time, the sum of registrations — goes deeper in [Patents & intellectual property](/kurser/v13-patent-ip) and in [the V13 patent analysis](/blogg/v13-patent-ip-analys).

## The commercial company — revenues, R&D and the multiple

The revenue side is read per product and geography. The share from the largest products is a concentration measure: a product accounting for half of revenues makes the whole company a single patent clock — the risk not visible in the P/E is taken up in [revenue diversification](/blogg/intaktsdiversifiering-risken-som-inte-syns-i-pe).

The research cost is the industry's investment, not a line to minimize: pharma companies normally spend 15–25 percent of revenues on research and development, and the R&D curve says something about how the pipeline is maintained. The multiple is compared within the industry — [the industry medians](/blogg/branschmedianer-akm2) show how healthcare key figures deviate from other sectors — always with the cliff calendar alongside.

## Cash, share issues and the value of the pipeline

The development company's equation has three variables: the cash, the burn and the catalyst calendar. Does the cash last to the next milestone? If not, the share issue comes — new shares diluting existing owners, the mechanics in [Emission risk](/kurser/rk-02-emissionrisk). Two dates are therefore read together: when the cash runs out, and when data is expected.

Put numbers on it with an imaginary company. Cash is SEK 1,200 million and the burn SEK 100 million per quarter — runway becomes 1,200 ÷ 100 = 12 quarters. The lead project's phase III data is expected in eight quarters: the window lasts with margin. Had data been expected in twelve or more quarters, the company would have had to raise capital again before the value-driving news — and share issues cost the most in uncertainty, precisely when the price is depressed by it.

The pipeline itself is valued as probability-weighted cash flows. Example with an imaginary project: the value at fully successful approval is estimated at SEK 20 billion; the project, in phase III with an assumed probability of approval of 70 percent, gets a risk-adjusted value of 20 × 0.7 = SEK 14 billion. Sum all projects, subtract debt and costs, compare with the market capitalization — that is the reasoning, in rough form. The probabilities are estimates and the answers sensitive to them; it is a method for structuring thought, not a machine that spits out an answer key.

## How to read the pharmaceutical company's report

- **Revenues per product and geography** — commercial companies; the bestseller share is the concentration measure.
- **The pipeline table** — phase per project, next milestone and expected date; the catalyst calendar.
- **Cash position and burn** — development companies; runway in quarters on the latest burn.
- **R&D cost as a percentage of revenues** — how the pipeline is maintained.
- **Partner agreements** — milestone payments are partly financing, partly confirmation that someone will pay for the project.
- **The patent list** — protection per product, with start and end dates.

Medical technology — companies manufacturing equipment and consumables, like Getinge and Elekta — has a shorter and cheaper approval chain than medicines, and is analyzed closer to industrial companies with a medical customer base. The whole sector's breadth is covered by [the Healthcare Sector](/kurser/km-048-halsovardsektorn).

## The summary

- Pharmaceutical stocks are two analyses: commercial companies on revenues and multiple with the patent clock alongside, development companies on pipeline, cash and runway.
- The development chain phases I–III take over a decade; roughly one in ten clinical projects reaches approval — the catalysts are binary.
- The patent gives a maximum of 20 years from application; effective exclusivity after development time is shorter, and the patent cliff can halve a product's revenues.
- The pipeline is valued as probability-weighted cash flows — structure for thinking, not an answer key.
- R&D share, product concentration and the catalyst calendar are the report's three own key figures.

Next step: [the Pharma Sector](/kurser/km-039-pharmasektorn) deepens every measure of the sector, and [Regulatory catalysts](/kurser/v18-regulatoriska) the event types that move prices.
